title: Norepinephrine extravasation: local phentolamine (alpha blockade)
vignette: A 67-year-old man admitted for right lower lobe pneumonia subsequently develops hypotension and lactic acidosis. He is started on a norepinephrine intravenous drip. A few hours later, the antecubital vein being used for the infusion blanches and the tissues surrounding the IV site become cold, hard, and pale. Local injection of the affected tissues with which of the following agents is most likely to be of greatest benefit?

clues.note: Norepinephrine is a potent alpha-1 agonist. If it leaks out of the vein (extravasation), intense local alpha-1 vasoconstriction can cause ischemic tissue necrosis.

clues.text: antecubital vein being used for the infusion blanches
clues.note: Blanching of the vein/skin along the infusion indicates the vasopressor is leaking and causing local vasoconstriction (extravasation).

clues.text: tissues surrounding the IV site become cold, hard, and pale
clues.note: Cold, hard, pale (indurated, blanched) tissue around the IV is the classic sign of norepinephrine extravasation with ischemia - treat with a local alpha blocker to vasodilate.

whatMatters: Norepinephrine (a potent alpha-1 agonist) has extravasated, causing intense local vasoconstriction and threatened ischemic necrosis (cold, hard, pale, blanched tissue). The antidote is local infiltration with PHENTOLAMINE, a nonselective alpha-adrenergic blocker that reverses the vasoconstriction. Answer B. Give within ~12 hours of extravasation.
strategy: Identify the problem (alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction from a leaked vasopressor), then counter it with an alpha blocker = phentolamine. Reject the others: calcium gluconate (hypocalcemia/hyperkalemia), heparin (thrombosis - but there's no clot here), isoproterenol (beta agonist - weaker at reversing alpha-1 constriction in skin), lidocaine (blocks sodium channels/nerves, not the vasoconstriction).

eliminations.label: Calcium gluconate - hypocalcemia/hyperkalemia
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: calcium gluconate treats severe hypocalcemia and stabilizes the myocardium in hyperkalemia. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it doesn't reverse alpha-1 vasoconstriction. ✅ Correct if: symptomatic hypocalcemia or hyperkalemia with ECG changes.

eliminations.label: Heparin - arterial thrombosis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: heparin is an anticoagulant for thrombosis. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the ischemia here is from vasospasm (extravasation), not a clot; there are no thrombosis risk factors. ✅ Correct if: cold, pulseless limb from arterial thrombosis (e.g., AFib embolus).

eliminations.label: Isoproterenol - beta agonist
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: isoproterenol is a nonselective beta agonist that causes some vasodilation (beta-2). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: subcutaneous skin vessels are relatively low in beta-2 vs alpha-1 receptors, so an alpha blocker is far more effective at reversing norepinephrine-induced vasoconstriction. ✅ Correct if: a scenario needing beta-agonist chronotropy/bronchodilation.

eliminations.label: Lidocaine - sodium-channel blocker
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: lidocaine blocks sodium channels (local anesthesia; also an antiarrhythmic). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it relaxes some vascular smooth muscle but does not reverse the alpha-1 vasoconstriction driving the ischemia. ✅ Correct if: local anesthesia or ventricular arrhythmia (not extravasation).

reasoning: Norepinephrine is a potent alpha-1 agonist; leaking out of the vein causes intense local vasoconstriction
Cold, hard, pale, blanched tissue around the IV = extravasation with threatened ischemic necrosis
Reverse the alpha-1 vasoconstriction with a local alpha blocker
mechanism: Norepinephrine is a potent alpha-1 adrenergic agonist used as a vasopressor. Extravasation (leakage into surrounding tissue) causes intense local alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction, producing blanching, induration, and cold, pale skin that can progress to ischemic tissue necrosis. The antidote is local infiltration of phentolamine, a nonselective (competitive) alpha-adrenergic antagonist, which blocks alpha-1 receptors to relax vascular smooth muscle and restore perfusion; it should be given within about 12 hours of extravasation to be effective. The distractors do not counter alpha-1 vasoconstriction: calcium gluconate treats hypocalcemia/hyperkalemia, heparin treats thrombosis (not vasospasm), isoproterenol is a beta agonist (skin vessels are relatively alpha-rich, so beta agonism is less effective), and lidocaine blocks sodium channels/nerve conduction rather than the vasoconstriction.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Pharm > adrenergic pharmacology: norepinephrine = alpha-1 agonist; phentolamine = nonselective alpha blocker; extravasation antidote.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Name the culprit (alpha-1 vasoconstriction) and choose the direct antagonist (alpha blocker = phentolamine).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on extravasation, alpha-1 vs beta-2 receptors, phentolamine, or induration? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Isoproterenol (beta agonist) and lidocaine cause some vasodilation but don't specifically reverse alpha-1 constriction; heparin/calcium address different problems.

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: norepinephrine extravasation (cold/pale/hard, blanched) -> local phentolamine (alpha blocker) within ~12 h.

memoryHook: Norepi leaked and clamped the vessels shut - blanch and freeze. Un-clamp with phentolamine (block the alpha, open the flow).
